{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=automated+scientific+discovery+problem+formulation+intrinsic+motivation+information+gain&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Discovering interpretable low-dimensional dynamics using maximum entropy.\", \"abstract\": \"Models (i.e., governing equations) are fundamental to science and engineering. Advances in data acquisition now make it possible to extract interpretable, low-dimensional descriptions from high-dimensional observations. However, existing approaches sacrifice either interpretability for reconstruction accuracy or infer symbolic dynamics without relating latent coordinates to physically meaningful observables. Here we present Edwin (maximum entropy-driven compression with interpretable nonlinear model discovery), a unified framework that simultaneously performs dimensionality reduction using the dynamic maximum entropy (DME) principle and discovers sparse symbolic models governing latent dynamics, as well as the coupling between learned features and external metadata. We validate Edwin on diverse simulated systems, including stochastic diffusion, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, self-assembling particles, and neural population firing rates, as well as on a noisy experimental time series of aggregating RNA-liposome complexes. Across all systems, Edwin recovers low-dimensional symbolic models that are physically interpretable and generalize to unseen conditions. Together, these results establish Edwin as a principled framework for inferring interpretable, low-dimensional dynamics from high-dimensional nonnegative data.\", \"doi\": \"10.1103/lkbs-j1by\", \"pmid\": \"42888767\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13679066\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1103/lkbs-j1by\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679066\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679066?p…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=autonomous+goal+formation+intrinsic+motivation+objective+discovery&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Human-Designed Objectives: Autonomous Goal Generation in AI Through Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Directed Agency\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Current artificial intelligence systems remain fundamentally constrained by their dependence on human-designed objectives and reward functions, limiting their capacity for genuine autonomy and open-ended development. This paper proposes Autonomous Goal Generation Networks (AGGNs), a theoretical framework for architectures that synthesize, evaluate, and pursue their own objectives through intrinsic motivation. The framework specifies five components: Goal-Generative Networks (GGNs, based on a VAE-style sampler over a goal embedding space), Objective Evaluation Systems (OESs) with six explicit criteria, Intrinsic Motivation Engines (IMEs) implementing curiosity, competence, empowerment, autonomy, and aesthetic drives, Autonomous Agency Controllers (AACs) for concurrent-objective scheduling, and Self-Reflective Goal Refinement (SRGR) for closing the loop. We prove a goal-distribution convergence result (Theorem 1) under stationary feedback and a stability condition for the SRGR loop. The contribution of this paper is theoretical: we identify the structural and motivational ingredients an autonomously-goal-generating agent must possess. No empirical validation is reported. Section VI specifies the protocol — benchmarks (Minecraft-like exploration, creative reasoning, robotic skill acquisition, scientific discovery, multi-agent social tasks), baselines (curiosity-driven exploration, empowerment maximization, novelty search), and metrics (goal diversity, coherence, achievement rate, exploration efficiency) — against which AGGNs should be evaluated.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1037/mot0000295.supp\", \"title\": [\"Supplemental Material for Autonomous Versus Controlled Goal Motivation Differentially Predicts Goal Progress and Well-Being Through Emotion Regulation Styles\"], \"URL\…

Abstract
Creative Problem Solving (CPS) is a sub-area within Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) that
focuses on methods for solving oﬀ-nominal, or anomalous problems in autonomous systems.
Despite many advancements in planning and learning, resolving novel problems or adapting
existing knowledge to a new context, especially in cases where the environment may
change in unpredictable ways post deployment, remains a limiting factor in the safe and
useful integration of intelligent systems. The emergence of increasingly autonomous systems
dictates the necessity for AI agents to deal with environmental uncertainty through creativity.
To stimulate further research in CPS, we present a deﬁnition and a framework of CPS,
which we adopt to categorize existing AI methods in this ﬁeld. Our framework consists of
four main components of a CPS problem, namely, 1) problem formulation, 2) knowledge
representation, 3) method of knowledge manipulation, and 4) method of evaluation. We
conclude our survey with open research questions, and suggested directions for the future.
